rows.stem: Caenorhabditis elegans is a nematode which is
rows.solution: Caenorhabditis elegans is a tiny roundworm that lives freely in the soil and causes no disease. It is one of the organisms whose complete genome was sequenced alongside the Human Genome Project (with bacteria, yeast, Drosophila, rice and Arabidopsis), and NCERT describes it as **a free living non-pathogenic nematode**. It is not a parasite of any host, inside or outside. So the answer is option (A) Free living and non-pathogenic.

rows.stem:
Self-incompatibility in some flowering plants is a _____ mechanism that prevents self-fertilization.
Fill in the blank with the appropriate option :
rows.solution: **Self-incompatibility** is an outbreeding device. It is a **genetic mechanism** that prevents pollen of the same flower, or of other flowers of the same plant, from fertilising the ovules: the pistil recognises its own pollen and stops it either from germinating on the stigma or from growing a pollen tube down the style. It works through genes, not through the shape or structure of the flower. So the answer is option (D) Genetic.

rows.stem: Which of the following traits studied by Mendel in pea plant is a recessive trait ?
rows.solution:
Of the seven pairs of contrasting traits Mendel studied in the garden pea, the dominant and recessive forms of the ones listed are:
- Stem height: **tall** is dominant over dwarf.
- Pod colour: **green** is dominant over yellow.
- Seed colour: **yellow** is dominant over green, so **green seed is recessive**.
- Flower colour: **violet** is dominant over white.

Tall stem, green pod and violet flower are all dominant forms. So the answer is option (C) Green seed.

rows.stem: Current percentage of tropical rainforests covering the Earth's land surface is
rows.solution: Tropical rain forests are among the richest stores of biodiversity, but they are being cleared fast for agriculture and other uses. They once covered **14 per cent** of the Earth's land surface and now cover **no more than 6 per cent**. The figure of 14% is the original cover, not the present one. So the answer is option (B) 6%.

rows.stem: Study the given pedigree and identify the disease represented.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a boxed three-generation pedigree in standard symbols (circles for females, squares for males): a couple at the top, their six children in the second generation, one of whom is married with three children in the third. Which individuals are shaded (affected) and their sexes decide the mode of inheritance and therefore the answer, so they are withheld here. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
In the pedigree, a couple who are both **unaffected** have an affected son and an affected daughter, and an unaffected daughter of theirs, married to an unaffected man, has an affected son.
- The trait skips a generation and appears in children of unaffected parents, so it is **recessive**: both parents must be carriers (heterozygous).
- An affected **daughter** born to an unaffected **father** rules out X-linked recessive inheritance, because for an X-linked recessive trait such a daughter must receive the faulty X from her father, who would then be affected. That excludes haemophilia and colour blindness.
- Down's syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (a chromosomal disorder), not by a recessive allele passed down a family in this way.

The trait is therefore **autosomal recessive**, and of the choices only sickle cell anaemia is inherited this way. So the answer is option (A) Sickle cell Anaemia.

rows.stem:
If any organ fails to function satisfactorily, transplantation is the only remedy to enable the patient to live a normal life.
All of the following are true w.r.t. transplantation except -

options.label: A
options.text: Tissue matching is essential before undertaking any graft.

options.label: B
options.text: T-lymphocytes play an important role in graft rejection.

options.label: C
options.text: Patient takes immuno-suppressants for first few weeks only after transplantation.

options.label: D
options.text: Blood group matching is important before transplantation.

rows.solution:
The question asks for the statement that is NOT true.
- Tissue matching and blood group matching are essential before any graft or transplant, so that the body does not reject it.
- Graft rejection is a **cell-mediated immune response**, and **T-lymphocytes** carry it out, because the body can tell self from non-self.
- The patient has to take **immuno-suppressants all his or her life**, not just for the first few weeks after the transplant. If the drugs are stopped, the immune system can still reject the organ.

So the false statement is the one that limits immuno-suppressants to the first few weeks. So the answer is option (C) Patient takes immuno-suppressants for first few weeks only after transplantation.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Under a particular set of selection pressure, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy.
Reason (R) : Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness in the habitat where they live.
rows.context: For Question numbers 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from Code (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not correct explanation for Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Organisms show different patterns of reproduction (life history variation). Populations evolve to **maximise their reproductive fitness**, also called Darwinian fitness (a high r value), in the habitat in which they live. Because of this, under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the **most efficient reproductive strategy**: for example, some breed only once in a lifetime (Pacific salmon fish, bamboo) and others many times; some produce a large number of small offspring (oysters, pelagic fishes) and others a small number of large offspring (birds, mammals). The Reason states the very principle that leads to what the Assertion describes. So both the Assertion and the Reason are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
A patent with Type I diabetes is unable to produce sufficient insulin.
(a) How has recombinant DNA technology helped in addressing this problem ?
(b) Mention its advantage over animal derived insulin.
rows.solution:
(a) Insulin is made of two short polypeptide chains, **chain A and chain B**, linked by disulphide bridges. In 1983 the American company **Eli Lilly** used recombinant DNA technology to make human insulin. It prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them into **plasmids of E. coli**. The bacteria produced the two chains separately; these were extracted and combined by creating **disulphide bonds** to form human insulin. This allows human insulin to be produced in large quantities for diabetic patients.

(b) Insulin used earlier was extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. This animal insulin caused some patients to develop **allergy or other reactions** to the foreign protein. Genetically engineered insulin is identical to human insulin and does not cause such reactions; it can also be produced in much larger quantities. (The paper prints "A patent with Type I diabetes"; a patient is meant.)

rows.stem:
Study the flow chart and answer the following questions :
Biofertilizers
\(\downarrow\)
| A | B | C |
|---|---|---|
| e.g. Glomus | e.g. Azospirillum | e.g. Rhizobium |
(a) Identify A, B and C in the flow chart.
(b) Give one another example of bio-fertilizer B.
rows.solution:
(a) The flow chart shows the three groups of biofertilisers, each with its example:
- **A: Mycorrhiza (fungi).** Glomus forms a symbiotic association with plant roots; the fungus absorbs phosphorus from the soil and passes it to the plant.
- **B: Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria.** Azospirillum lives freely in the soil and fixes atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil.
- **C: Symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria.** Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms the plant can use.

(b) Another free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium used as a biofertiliser is **Azotobacter**.

rows.stem:
Explain the type of interaction between :
(i) Egret and Cattle
(ii) Cuckoo and Crow
rows.solution:
(i) **Egret and cattle: commensalism.** One species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited. Cattle egrets forage close to grazing cattle: as the cattle move through the vegetation they stir up and flush out insects that would otherwise be difficult for the egrets to find and catch. The egret benefits; the cattle are not affected.

(ii) **Cuckoo and crow: brood parasitism**, a form of parasitism. The cuckoo (koel) lays its eggs in the nest of the crow, its host, and lets the crow incubate them. The cuckoo's eggs have evolved to resemble the crow's eggs in size and colour, which reduces the chance of the host detecting the foreign eggs and throwing them out. The cuckoo benefits and the crow is harmed, since it spends its effort raising another bird's young.

rows.subtopic: Species Numbers and Patterns of Biodiversity
rows.stem: Biodiversity exists at various levels within an ecosystem. Explain biodiversity at genetic and ecological level.
rows.solution:
- **Genetic diversity:** a single species may show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range. The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria, growing in different Himalayan ranges, shows genetic variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical **reserpine** it produces. India has more than **50,000** genetically different strains of rice and **1,000** varieties of mango.
- **Ecological diversity:** this is diversity at the ecosystem level. India, with its **deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows**, has a far greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

rows.stem:
(a) Compare homologous and analogous organs by giving any one point of difference.
(b) Mention the type of evolution each represents and give one example of each from plants and animals.
rows.solution:
(a) One difference between them (any one is enough):

| Homologous organs | Analogous organs |
|---|---|
| Have the same basic anatomical structure but are modified to perform different functions | Are not similar in structure but perform similar functions |
| Have a common ancestry | Do not have a common ancestry |

(b) **Homologous organs show divergent evolution** (one ancestral structure modified in different directions), while **analogous organs show convergent evolution** (different structures coming to serve the same function).
- Homologous organs: in plants, the **thorns of Bougainvillea and the tendrils of Cucurbita**; in animals, the **forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and humans**, which share the same pattern of bones (vertebrate hearts and brains are other examples).
- Analogous organs: in plants, **sweet potato (a root modification) and potato (a stem modification)**, both storing food; in animals, the **wings of a butterfly and of a bird** (others: the eye of the octopus and of mammals, the flippers of penguins and dolphins).

rows.stem:
In the given diagram – 'A' is an embryonic stage that gets transformed into 'B', which in turn gets implanted in the endometrium of human female.
(i) (1) Identify A, B, C and D.
(2) State the fate of 'C' immediately after implantation.
(3) Name the special cells found in 'C' and their function.
(ii) What is the role of oxytocin during parturition ? Where is it released from ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a boxed drawing of two embryonic stages, A on the left and B on the right, joined by an arrow captioned 'Transforms into'; on B two pointer lines are labelled C and D. What A and B look like, and which parts of B the labels C and D mark, are what (i)(1) asks the student to identify, so they are withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) (1) The drawing shows the human embryo before implantation:
- **A: Morula**, the solid ball of 8 to 16 blastomeres formed by cleavage of the zygote.
- **B: Blastocyst**, formed as the morula divides further; its blastomeres are arranged into an outer layer and an inner group of cells.
- **C: Inner cell mass**, the group of cells attached to the trophoblast inside the blastocyst.
- **D: Trophoblast**, the outer layer of cells, which gets attached to the endometrium during implantation.

(2) Immediately after implantation, the **inner cell mass differentiates into the embryo**. It differentiates into an outer layer, the **ectoderm**, and an inner layer, the **endoderm**, and a **mesoderm** soon appears between them. These three germ layers give rise to all the tissues and organs of the adult.

(3) The inner cell mass contains certain cells called **stem cells**, which have the **potency to give rise to all the tissues and organs** of the body.

(ii) At the end of pregnancy, signals from the fully developed foetus and the placenta induce mild uterine contractions (the foetal ejection reflex), which trigger the release of **oxytocin from the maternal pituitary** (the posterior pituitary). Oxytocin acts on the **uterine muscle** and causes **stronger uterine contractions**, which in turn stimulate still more oxytocin secretion. This continuing cycle of contractions leads to the expulsion of the baby out of the uterus through the birth canal, which is parturition.

rows.stem:
Sexually transmitted infections are a major threat to our society. So it is said that "Prevention is better than cure".
(i) Write the three simple principles to be followed to prevent such infections.
(ii) How can sex education programs in schools help in improving reproductive health ? (4 points)
rows.solution:
(i) Sexually transmitted infections can be prevented by following three simple principles:
- **Avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners.**
- **Always use condoms during coitus.**
- **In case of doubt, go to a qualified doctor for early detection** and get complete treatment if diagnosed with an infection.

(ii) Sex education in schools improves reproductive health in many ways (any four):
- It discourages children from believing in **myths and misconceptions** about sex-related problems.
- It gives **proper information about the reproductive organs**, adolescence and the related changes.
- It teaches **safe and hygienic sexual practices**.
- It gives proper information about **sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**, how they spread and how they can be prevented.
- Information about **AIDS** helps people, especially those in the adolescent age group, to lead a reproductively healthy life.
